text: Dedication of the IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (ASCC), also known as the Harvard Mark I.
William N. Papian writes a thesis proposal for work on magnetic devices needed for Forrester’s proposed three-dimensional memory array.
J. W. Forrester initiates ferrite material development work at MIT based on square-loop magnetic ferrite materials reported by Albers-Schönberg in 1949.
Whirlwind achieves 90 percent useful operation using electrostatic storage-tube memories.
A 2×2×2 ferrite core memory built in Haynes’s group at IBM operates in the XY selection, 3D mode.
The first bank of 32×32×17 bit ferrite core memory is removed from the MTC and placed in Whirlwind I.
The first 64×64×17 bit ferrite core array is operational in the MTC at MIT.
International Telemeter installs a 4096 word ferrite core memory on the Rand Corporation’s Johnniac computer, and ERA ships a 32×32×36 bit memory on its 1103 computer to the National Security Agency.
The XD-1 SAGE prototype computer with two 64×64×36 bit arrays is shipped by IBM to Lincoln Laboratory.
The core threading machine is first used in production at IBM about this time. It reduces XY core threading time from twenty-five hours to twelve minutes.
IBM agrees to buy 90 million CuMn ferrite cores from Ferroxcube (a Philips subsidiary) at an average price of 1.5 cents each.
Research Corporation offers to license IBM under Forrester’s patent at two cents per core. IBM rejects price as too high.
The Hursley Laboratory is asked to develop CCROS in addition to TROS for the IBM System/360.
